title: Περιστερὰ διψῶσα
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 301 (= Perry 201). Text as printed. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Περιστερὰ δίψει συνεχομένη, ὡς ἐθεάσατο ἔν τινι πίνακι κρατῆρα ὕδατος γεγραμμένον, ὑπέλαβεν ἀληθινὸν εἶναι.
sentences.tr: Peristera dipsei synechomenē, hōs etheasato en tini pinaki kratēra hydatos gegrammenon, hypelaben alēthinon einai.
sentences.l: A dove, held fast by thirst, when she saw a mixing-bowl of water painted on a panel, took it to be real.
sentences.n: συνέχομαι with the dative is to be gripped by a thing — hunger, thirst, disease — and held in its hold. γράφω covers writing and painting alike, and a πίναξ is the board painted on. ὑπολαμβάνω is to take a thing to be so, with no warrant beyond one's own supposition.

sentences.t: Διόπερ πολλῷ ῥοίζῳ ἐνεχθεῖσα ἔλαθεν ἑαυτὴν τῷ πίνακι ἐντινάξασα.
sentences.tr: Dioper pollōi rhoizōi enechtheisa elathen heautēn tōi pinaki entinaxasa.
sentences.l: Wherefore, having been borne on with a great rush, she escaped her own notice dashing herself against the panel.
sentences.i: And so she came on with a great rush of wings, and before she knew it had dashed herself against the panel.
sentences.n: λανθάνω with a supplementary participle puts the deed in the participle and the not-noticing in the verb: she did the dashing without knowing she did it, and the same construction returns in this fable's moral. ῥοῖζος is the whistling rush of an arrow or of wings. ἐνεχθεῖσα is the aorist passive participle of φέρω.

sentences.t: Συνέβη δὲ αὐτῇ, τῶν πτερῶν περιθραυσθέντων, ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς καταπεσοῦσαν ὑπό τινος τῶν παρατυχόντων συλληφθῆναι.
sentences.tr: Synebē de autēi, tōn pterōn perithrausthentōn, epi tēs gēs katapesousan hypo tinos tōn paratychontōn syllēphthēnai.
sentences.l: And it befell her, her wings having been broken all about, having fallen down upon the ground, to be seized by one of those who chanced to be there.
sentences.i: And so it befell her that, her wings broken about her, she fell to the ground and was taken by one of the bystanders.
sentences.n: συμβαίνει takes the dative of the person and an infinitive of what happens to him. καταπεσοῦσαν is accusative, agreeing with the unexpressed subject of that infinitive even though the dove has just been named in the dative αὐτῇ; Greek shifts case here without discomfort. οἱ παρατυχόντες are those who happened to be on the spot.

sentences.t: Οὕτως ἔνιοι τῶν ἀνθρώπων διὰ σφοδρὰς ἐπιθυμίας ἀπροσκέπτως τοῖς πράγμασιν ἐπιχειροῦντες λανθάνουσιν ἑαυτοὺς εἰς ὄλεθρον εἰσιέντες.
sentences.tr: Houtōs enioi tōn anthrōpōn dia sphodras epithymias aproskeptōs tois pragmasin epicheirountes lanthanousin heautous eis olethron eisientes.
sentences.l: Thus some among men, through violent desires setting their hand to affairs without looking about them, escape their own notice going into ruin.
sentences.i: Thus some men, out of violent desire, take a thing in hand without looking about them, and are walking into their own ruin before they know it.
sentences.n: The same λανθάνω construction as in the body, and it is the moral's whole point: the ruin is not stumbled into but walked into, unseen.
